idiom_name: nil with safe navigation (&.) / Object#try, or a small NullFoo singleton
implementation_notes: Ruby's nil is a real object with neutral protocol behaviour - nil.to_s is '', nil.to_a is [], nil.nil? is true - but it is not a null object for your own interface: customer.name on nil still raises NoMethodError, and the standard analysis of the idiom states plainly that NilClass does not qualify. The language's idiomatic answer is therefore safe navigation (logger&.info(...), Ruby 2.3+) or ActiveSupport's Object#try, which returns nil instead of raising; when the collaborator must be non-null, the pattern is written in three lines as a constant singleton (NullLogger.instance) or as a method_missing-based do-nothing object. Choose the null object when callers should not branch at all; keep &. when absence is a case the caller can see.
code_sketch:
class NullLogger
  def self.instance = (@instance ||= new)
  def info(*) = nil            # same interface, no output
end

class Service
  def initialize(logger = NullLogger.instance) = @logger = logger
  def run = @logger.info("running")          # no &. needed
end
# absence visible instead: @logger&.info("running")
pitfalls: 'logger || NullLogger.instance' replaces a legitimate false as well as nil; use a keyword default or an explicit nil check.
A method_missing-based do-nothing object answers every message, so a misspelled method silently succeeds; respond only to the protocol's methods, or define them explicitly.
A Ruby null object is truthy: 'if null_customer' runs, and ActiveSupport's blank?/present? are false for nil but true for your null object unless you override them.
